verification.competitor_check: Independently checked the primary landscape through 2026-08-24, including arXiv:2503.02809, arXiv:2510.17506, arXiv:2604.19740, and arXiv:2606.30930 against official arXiv and proceedings records.

question: Can constant-step gradient descent beyond the classical local stability scale converge on homogeneous matrix factorization while selecting flatter, more balanced factorizations?

key_findings.claim: The paper identifies a real and useful discrete-time mechanism: a sufficiently large stable step can reduce factor imbalance that gradient flow would approximately preserve.
key_findings.evidence: For scalar factorization, the dynamics are divided into a searching phase, where the sum of squared factor norms decreases over one or two steps, and a converging phase near a flatter portion of the minimizer manifold. The experiments consistently show initially unbalanced factors becoming closer in norm as the step approaches the empirically stable boundary, while small-step runs retain their initial imbalance.

key_findings.claim: The proved unconditional convergence scope is narrow: scalar factorization and rank-one approximation of an isotropic matrix, not arbitrary matrix factorization or neural networks.
key_findings.evidence: Theorems 3.1-3.2 treat n=1 with any factor width; Theorems 4.1-4.3 treat d=1 and A=mu I. For arbitrary n, d, and A, Theorem 5.1 explicitly assumes that GD already converges to a point and only attempts to constrain the limiting point. The conclusion acknowledges a substantial gap to deep linear and nonlinear networks, and the matrix-sensing and matrix-completion extensions are empirical only.

key_findings.claim: The phase-one proof does not establish finite entrance into the claimed convergence region.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma G.5 only excludes convergence to sharp fixed points above the 2/h curvature boundary for almost every initialization. Lemma G.7 then treats this as proof that an infinite phase-one trajectory cannot occur, asserting that one- or two-step decreases are bounded below except near two surfaces. In the near-surface case its decrement depends on a moving epsilon_k and no uniform lower bound, summability argument, or exclusion of other omega-limit sets is supplied. The paper itself exhibits periodic orbits at large steps in Appendix B, so ruling out non-fixed bounded behavior is indispensable rather than automatic.

key_findings.claim: The phase-two scalar convergence argument is largely qualitative and does not close several recurrence and invariance claims needed for Theorem 3.1.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma G.10 invokes prior phase-one reasoning to assert bounded return in a number of steps independent of iteration without deriving such a uniform return time. Lemma G.11 repeatedly asserts existence of later indices, lower bounds away from zero, and permanence in a monotone region from decreases of different quantities, but does not present a single Lyapunov function, compactness-plus-limit-set argument, or complete case invariant. Its final contraction constants depend on the current residual, and the proof does not rigorously rule out repeated transitions among the listed regions.

anchors.section: Appendix G.2 / Lemmas G.17-G.20 across pages 29-30

key_findings.claim: The rank-one isotropic extension inherits the scalar gaps and adds unsupported alignment-to-point-convergence steps.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma H.3 says the extra misalignment term yields constant decrease when bounded away from zero, then assumes a finite K and a favorable c1 without proving the trajectory must satisfy the required alternative. Lemma H.4 argues that a merely bounded extra term prevents convergence, which does not follow. Later, convergence of x_k^T y_k to mu and |cos angle(x_k,y_k)| to one only gives convergence to the minimizer manifold; it does not by itself show that the vector directions or the full iterates converge to one point. The proof even prints |cos angle| to zero immediately before claiming alignment, contradicting Theorem 4.1 and Lemma H.9.

anchors.section: Appendix H.2 / transition to Lemma H.9

key_findings.claim: The general-rank proof of Theorem 5.1 contains a fatal circular scaling assumption and an invalid rank inference.
key_findings.evidence: At a global minimum the proof says that ||A||_F=O(1) allows one to take ||X||_F and ||Y||_F as O(1). Homogeneity makes this false: X can be multiplied by any a and Y by a^-1 while preserving XY^T, producing arbitrarily large factor norms. That is precisely the imbalance the theorem seeks to bound. It then infers that the number N of nonzero Hessian eigenvalues is O(n) from tr(M^2)=O(n); a bounded squared trace supplies no such upper bound on rank. These steps are needed to lower-bound lambda_max by a dimension-independent multiple of ||X||_F^2+||Y||_F^2.

key_findings.claim: Theorem I.4's final constant step does not follow even from the preceding spectral inequality.
key_findings.evidence: The proof obtains c0(||X||_F^2+||Y||_F^2)<=2/h for one lower-bound constant c0. It then states that choosing c(n,d)>c0 makes the same inequality hold. Increasing the multiplier strengthens the inequality and is not implied. A valid c could be defined from an exact eigenvalue-to-norm ratio only after proving it is uniform over all relevant global minima; the paper supplies neither that definition nor such a compactness argument.

key_findings.claim: Appendix I additionally misstates the rank-one fixed-point block condition and contradicts itself about the balancing constant's dimension dependence.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem I.1 states the block-norm product condition for every distinct singular-value block and indexes the blocks through n, although the setup defines m blocks and the proof immediately shows that at most one block can be active when the mu_i are distinct. Appendix I.3 then says the final constant is independent of n, r, d, and h, contradicting Theorem I.4's c=c(n,d) and the dimension-dependent argument preceding it.

anchors.section: Appendix I.1 / Theorem I.1 statement and proof

key_findings.claim: The stability-to-almost-everywhere argument is stated too loosely for non-isolated minimizer and saddle manifolds.
key_findings.evidence: The paper repeatedly says that each unstable fixed point has a negligible stable set and therefore almost every convergent initialization reaches a stable global minimum. Matrix factorization has continua of stationary points and symmetry-induced unit Jacobian eigenvalues. Showing each individual basin is null does not make an uncountable union null, and the quoted strict-stability proposition requires every eigenvalue modulus to be below one, which global minimizers violate along symmetry directions. A center-stable manifold or strict-saddle-avoidance theorem with map invertibility and a dimension count is needed but not provided.

key_findings.claim: Two supporting mathematical statements are misstated or algebraically inconsistent.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem F.3 concludes that iterates converge to a stationary point from the standard descent inequality, but its proof establishes only ||grad f(x_k)|| to zero; iterate convergence requires additional assumptions. In Appendix I.2, both diagonal blocks of M^2 contain a residual product, so their traces contribute 2d||A-XY^T||_F^2 in total, while the displayed formula includes only d times that residual. The missing factor does not repair the later rank error but confirms the general-rank calculation is not exact.

anchors.section: Appendix I.2 / blocks of M squared
Appendix I.2 / trace of M squared

key_findings.claim: The experiments illustrate the phenomenon but do not validate a quantitative theory or a generalization benefit.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 1-14 plot factor norms and training loss for selected synthetic initializations and hand-chosen fractions of a stability-limit step. No uncertainty, repeated-trial distribution, seed, numerical table, convergence tolerance, or comparison of predicted versus observed bound is reported. Matrix sensing uses only 10 random measurements of 100 by 100 factors with independent random targets, and matrix completion uses one small synthetic instance; these demonstrate norm motion rather than recovery. No test risk or neural-network generalization is measured.

key_findings.claim: The paper is not computationally reproducible from an author artifact.
key_findings.evidence: The 45-page ICLR/arXiv source provides figures and extensive proofs but no code link, repository, data file, environment, pseudocode implementation, seeds, or machine-readable results. The official arXiv record lists only PDF and TeX source, author pages link the paper but no artifact, and exact-title, identifier, and GitHub searches found only third-party indexes offering to request code.

method.core_idea: Treat finite-step gradient descent as a discrete dynamical system whose local stability cutoff excludes sharp, highly unbalanced representatives of a homogeneous minimizer manifold.
method.mechanism: For f(X,Y)=||A-XY^T||_F^2/2, the paper first solves scalar factorization by tracking u_k^2=||x_k||^2+||y_k||^2 and the multiplicative residual factor s_k, partitioning state space into a search phase and a convergence phase. It extends the recurrence with alignment variables U=x^T y, V=||x||^2, and W=||y||^2 for rank-one approximation of A=mu I. For arbitrary A and rank, it rotates by an SVD to a nonnegative diagonal target, vectorizes the GD map, and attempts to use Jacobian/Hessian stability at any converged global minimum to bound total factor norm and rotated factor difference by quantities proportional to 1/h.
assumptions: The optimized loss is unregularized squared Frobenius matrix factorization with square A in the main formulation.
Gradient descent is deterministic, simultaneous in both factors, and uses one constant learning rate h.
Scalar factorization assumes a positive target mu and excludes an unspecified Lebesgue-null set of initial conditions.
The rank-one convergence theorem assumes A=mu I and h<=min{4/(||x0||^2+||y0||^2+4sqrt(7)mu),1/(2sqrt(7)mu)}.
The general-matrix balancing theorem is conditional on GD converging to a point.
The singular values of A and its Frobenius norm are treated as controlled, with ||A||_F independent of n and d in the general-rank proof.
Almost-everywhere conclusions assume unstable stationary manifolds have null attraction basins under the GD map.
The selected converged global minimum is assumed to be dynamically stable in every non-symmetry direction.
Synthetic experiments use hand-selected random Gaussian matrices, initial norm ratios, and learning rates near an empirically chosen stability boundary.

techniques.role: Divides scalar GD dynamics into searching, oscillatory, and monotone-convergence regions.
Tracks x_k^T y_k-mu through a scalar multiplier s_k to distinguish transversal and unilateral convergence.
Uses ||x||^2+||y||^2 and ||x-y||^2 as curvature and imbalance surrogates on the minimizer manifold.
Tracks U, V, W and the Gram determinant VW-U^2 for rank-one isotropic approximation.
Attempts to pull measure-zero exceptional sets backward through the discrete GD map.
Reduces arbitrary square A to nonnegative diagonal D while preserving factor Frobenius norms.
Relates the Jacobian eigenvalues of the GD map at a stationary point to the 2/h sharpness cutoff.
Sweeps selected step-size fractions and initialization norm ratios for matrix factorization, sensing, and completion.

evaluations.setting: Scalar factorization with target mu=1 and factor widths up to 100
evaluations.metric: Factor norms, their final gap, training loss, and qualitative monotonicity
evaluations.result: Large stable steps produce a search-then-converge trajectory and much smaller final imbalance than small steps in the displayed runs
evaluations.baseline: Smaller fractions of the same initialization-dependent step bound

evaluations.setting: General overparameterized factorization with A in R^(6x6) and X,Y in R^(6x100)
evaluations.metric: Frobenius norms of factors and training loss over iterations
evaluations.result: Selected large steps balance the factor norms more strongly while still converging; the largest displayed step can diverge
evaluations.baseline: Five smaller step fractions for the same synthetic instance

evaluations.setting: Underparameterized factorization with A in R^(100x100) and rank-three factors
evaluations.metric: Factor Frobenius norms and shifted training loss
evaluations.result: The qualitative balancing trend persists in two selected initial norm ratios

evaluations.setting: Synthetic matrix sensing with 10 Gaussian measurements and X,Y in R^(100x6)
evaluations.result: Larger convergent steps reduce the factor-norm gap, but no ground-truth recovery or statistical error is measured

evaluations.setting: Synthetic 10x10 rank-two matrix completion at reported sparsity 0.6
evaluations.metric: Factor norms and observed-entry training objective
evaluations.result: Larger convergent steps yield more similar factor norms on one instance

evaluations.setting: Scalar stress tests near and beyond the stable step boundary
evaluations.metric: Loss, modified-equation trajectory error, and periodic orbits
evaluations.result: One step at the proposed upper bound converges, a slightly larger one diverges, a first-order modified equation fails to track GD, and period-2, -3, and -4 examples occur
evaluations.baseline: A slightly smaller or larger constant step and the first-order modified ODE

limitations: The phase-one scalar proof does not exclude infinite bounded trajectories outside the target region.
The phase-two scalar proof relies on qualitative case transitions and unproved uniform return or invariance claims.
The rank-one isotropic extension inherits those gaps and does not prove convergence of vector directions to a single point.
The general-rank proof assumes bounded factor norms despite homogeneity allowing arbitrarily unbalanced global minima.
The inference from tr(M^2)=O(n) to O(n) nonzero Hessian eigenvalues is invalid.
The Hessian squared-trace formula omits one of the two residual-block contributions.
The final replacement of c0 by a larger c(n,d) strengthens an inequality and is unsupported.
Theorem I.1 states mutually incompatible fixed-point conditions across every distinct singular-value block and uses n where the block index runs through m.
Appendix I.3 calls the balancing constant dimension-independent although Theorem I.4 defines it as c(n,d).
Almost-everywhere saddle avoidance is not proved for continua of non-isolated stationary points and symmetry-induced unit eigenvalues.
Theorem F.3 confuses convergence of gradient norms to zero with convergence of iterates.
Theorem 5.1 is conditional on convergence and supplies no general-matrix convergence rate or basin guarantee.
The unconditional theory covers only scalar factorization and rank-one approximation of isotropic A.
The paper studies deterministic full-batch GD, not SGD, momentum, schedules, or adaptive optimizers used in the motivating neural-network practice.
No theorem connects balancing or local Hessian flatness to test error or statistical generalization.
Flatness and balance are parameterization-dependent under homogeneous rescaling and are not compared with function-space complexity.
Matrix sensing and completion extensions are empirical single-instance demonstrations rather than proved results.
Experiments report no seeds, repeated-trial variance, numerical tables, convergence tolerances, or quantitative bound checks.
There is no neural-network experiment despite neural-network generalization motivating the work.
No author code, data, environment, or machine-readable result artifact is available.
failure_modes: A bounded phase-one orbit approaches neither a sharp fixed point nor the target ball, a case Lemma G.5 does not exclude.
One- and two-step norm decreases shrink toward zero, so infinitely many steps occur without crossing the 2/h boundary.
The iterate repeatedly switches among the scalar proof's case regions and avoids every locally monotone argument.
The inner product and alignment converge while vector directions drift along the non-isolated minimizer manifold.
An uncountable family of unstable stationary points has a union of stable sets that is not shown null.
A symmetry direction gives Jacobian eigenvalue one, so strict fixed-point stability propositions do not apply.
Homogeneous rescaling makes one factor arbitrarily large while preserving the same global product, invalidating the assumed O(1) factor norms.
The Hessian has many small nonzero eigenvalues: tr(M^2) remains O(n) although its rank grows with nd.
The spectral lower-bound constant depends on the particular minimizer or factor scaling rather than only n and d.
A learning rate just beyond the displayed boundary diverges or enters a periodic orbit instead of selecting a flat minimum.
Norm balancing improves while product recovery, held-out error, or downstream generalization worsens or remains undefined.
A hand-selected stability limit and initialization make a qualitative sweep look systematic despite substantial seed sensitivity.
Matrix sensing interpolates ten arbitrary observations without recovering any meaningful target matrix.
A third party can reproduce the equations but not the plotted instances because code, seeds, and raw outputs are absent.

competitive_landscape.title: Algorithmic Regularization in Learning Deep Homogeneous Models: Layers are Automatically Balanced
competitive_landscape.difference: Du, Hu, and Lee show that gradient flow preserves differences of squared layer norms and analyze diminishing or small positive steps for asymmetric factorization. The audited paper's distinctive proposal is that a much larger finite step actively shrinks pre-existing imbalance rather than merely preserving a balanced initialization, but its extension to deep homogeneous networks remains conjectural.

competitive_landscape.title: The large learning rate phase of deep learning: the catapult mechanism
competitive_landscape.difference: Lewkowycz et al. characterize a narrow stable large-learning-rate phase in solvable wide-network dynamics and validate catapult behavior and flatter convergence on practical networks. The audited paper supplies a different exact factorization recurrence, but offers no comparable neural-network evaluation or test-performance result.

competitive_landscape.title: Noisy Gradient Descent Converges to Flat Minima for Nonconvex Matrix Factorization
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. use injected perturbations to select a noise-determined flat global optimum from arbitrary initialization. The audited work isolates deterministic finite-step effects instead, but its general-rank stability proof is incomplete and its convergence result is far narrower.

competitive_landscape.title: Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Asymmetric Low-Rank Matrix Factorization
competitive_landscape.difference: Ye and Du prove polynomial-rate global convergence from random initialization for asymmetric low-rank factorization without a balancing regularizer. Their step is in a conventional controlled regime and does not establish large-step selection, while the audited paper's arbitrary-A theorem assumes convergence and therefore does not supersede this guarantee.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of the Step Size in Linear Diagonal Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Nacson et al. use dynamic stability to show that a large stable step can move diagonal linear regression from kernel-like to sparsity-inducing rich behavior and prove a sparse-regression generalization consequence. It makes the audited paper's missing bridge from parameter flatness to generalization especially salient.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Gradient Descent on the Edge of Stability in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Arora, Li, and Panigrahi derive an implicit flow along a minimizer manifold that reduces top Hessian curvature in stylized normalized-GD and transformed-loss settings. Their framework directly analyzes motion along non-isolated minima, the step that the audited paper assumes rather than proves in its rank-one alignment argument.

competitive_landscape.title: Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Damian, Nichani, and Lee use a cubic local expansion to explain how an unstable top-Hessian direction lowers curvature and makes GD track sharpness-constrained projected dynamics, with explicit predictions checked on standard models. This provides a more general local mechanism than factor norm balancing, though under its own regularity and scale-separation assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: Special Properties of Gradient Descent with Large Learning Rates
competitive_landscape.difference: Mohtashami, Jaggi, and Stich prove on constructed nonconvex classes that large-step full-batch GD can escape local minima that small-step GD does not, then separate this effect from stochastic noise in neural-network experiments. It broadens the discrete-time benefit beyond homogeneous balance and supplies practical validation absent here.

competitive_landscape.title: Good regularity creates large learning rate implicit biases: edge of stability, balancing, and catapult
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. place balancing, catapult, and edge-of-stability behavior in one regularity-based family of non-globally-smooth nonconvex objectives and add a non-asymptotic convergence-rate claim plus neural-network experiments. It is the natural successor to the audited paper, while still acknowledging theory for only specific functions.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Dynamics of Deep Linear Networks Beyond the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Ghosh et al. analyze deep linear matrix factorization beyond the edge of stability, including period doubling, low-dimensional oscillation subspaces, and monotone decay of the inter-layer balancing gap at a two-period orbit. It directly extends the phenomenon from two factors converging to a point toward deeper networks and persistent oscillatory regimes that the audited proof does not cover.

competitive_landscape.title: A Minimalist Example of Edge-of-Stability and Progressive Sharpening
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. prove progressive sharpening, self-stabilization, and non-asymptotic behavior along the entire GD trajectory for a two-layer width-one network with a two-dimensional input. It supplies the kind of rigorous entry and recurrence control missing from the audited scalar and rank-one phase arguments, while remaining a deliberately low-dimensional model.

competitive_landscape.title: Convergence Rates for Gradient Descent on the Edge of Stability in Overparametrised Least Squares
competitive_landscape.difference: MacDonald et al. decompose dynamics tangent and normal to a global-minimizer manifold and prove rates in subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes, including convergence toward a period-two orbit. This directly addresses the audited paper's missing control of tangential motion, finite entry, and non-fixed limit sets in an overparameterized least-squares setting.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalization at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Tuci et al. model stochastic optimizers as random dynamical systems, define a sharpness dimension using the full Hessian spectrum, and prove a corresponding generalization bound with MLP and Transformer experiments. It provides a direct, spectrum-wide bridge to generalization that the audited paper motivates but neither proves nor measures.

competitive_landscape.title: SGD at the Edge of Stability: Stochastic Stabilization with Large Learning Rates
competitive_landscape.difference: Emmanouilidis et al. prove repeated stochastic self-stabilization and best-iterate convergence for multiclass cross-entropy in linear classifiers and two-layer networks. It advances the SGD and realistic-loss directions absent from the audited deterministic matrix-factorization theory and explicitly controls returns from unstable to stable regimes.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Constant large-learning-rate GD can converge well beyond the usual 2/L scale and implicitly select flatter, more balanced solutions of homogeneous matrix factorization, with a broad general-matrix balancing theorem and numerical support.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper's clearest novel element is the explicit two-phase discrete recurrence for scalar factorization and the demonstration that finite steps can destroy gradient-flow balance invariants in a favorable direction. Prior work already studied automatic balancing under infinitesimal or small steps, noise-selected flat matrix factors, and catapult dynamics. The paper does not establish its most general claim: the arbitrary-rank proof is circular about bounded factors, makes an invalid Hessian-rank inference, and mishandles its final constant. The unconditional scalar and isotropic rank-one proofs also contain material limit-set and convergence gaps.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: This is an influential hypothesis-generating study of finite-step implicit bias, not a dependable general convergence theorem as written. Its qualitative message—that the discretization itself can favor stable, low-curvature representatives of a homogeneous solution class—has been strengthened by later edge-of-stability and deep-linear-network work. Reuse the scalar recurrence, experimental phenomenon, and stability heuristic; do not cite Theorem 5.1 as a rigorous arbitrary-matrix balancing guarantee without a repaired proof.

reusable_insights: Compare finite-step GD with gradient flow through invariants that discretization breaks, not only through a modified ODE.
On a homogeneous minimizer manifold, express sharpness in terms of factor imbalance and test the local stability cutoff 2/h.
Separate unconditional convergence, convergence conditional on entering a region, and properties conditional on convergence to a point.
When phase arguments use one- or two-step decrease, prove a uniform decrement or apply a summability and limit-set theorem near boundary surfaces.
Ruling out convergence to bad fixed points does not rule out cycles, quasiperiodic orbits, or other bounded omega-limit sets.
Convergence of distance to a minimizer manifold does not imply convergence of iterates to one minimizer; control tangential motion explicitly.
For continua of stationary points, use center-stable manifolds and a dimension argument rather than unioning pointwise null basins.
Never assume factor norms are bounded from a bounded product in a homogeneous factorization.
A bound on tr(H^2) does not upper-bound rank; track rank algebraically or use an effective-rank inequality in the correct direction.
Check whether a proposed larger constant strengthens or weakens the final inequality before replacing a proven constant.
Measure function-space recovery or generalization separately from parameter norm balance.
Include periodic-orbit and divergence maps when presenting a narrow stable large-step window.
Report seeds, trial distributions, stability-threshold selection, convergence criteria, and predicted-versus-observed bounds for synthetic dynamics.
Use matrix sensing and completion only as external-validity evidence after measuring recovery, not merely training interpolation and norm motion.
open_questions: Can Theorem 3.1 be repaired with a global Lyapunov function or a complete classification of omega-limit sets inside its stated step range?
Do any positive-measure initial conditions within the scalar theorem's step bound approach cycles or non-fixed bounded sets?
What additional argument proves convergence of factor directions, rather than only alignment and distance to the minimizer manifold, in the isotropic rank-one case?
Can center-stable manifold theory rigorously justify almost-everywhere convergence selection for the non-isolated stationary manifolds of matrix factorization?
What is the exact Hessian rank and spectrum at arbitrary-rank global minima after accounting for factor symmetries and residual directions?
Is there a uniform dimension-dependent constant relating largest Hessian eigenvalue to total factor norm over all global minimizers, and what is its sharp value?
Can the general-rank balancing statement be proved without assuming convergence or bounded factor norms?
How does the stable large-step interval depend on the complete singular spectrum, rank mismatch, and initialization orientation?
When do large steps converge to a point, a two-cycle, higher-period orbit, or chaos in deep matrix factorization?
Does balancing improve matrix recovery, robustness, or held-out risk after controlling for the represented product?
How does finite-step balancing interact with noise, momentum, adaptive preconditioning, weight decay, and learning-rate schedules?
Can the mechanism be established for multi-layer homogeneous ReLU networks with realistic data rather than inferred from two-factor linear models?
Which parameterization-invariant complexity measure should replace raw Hessian sharpness when comparing homogeneous solutions?
Would releasing exact experimental code reveal seed-sensitive failures near the claimed stability boundary?
reviewer_notes: Read the exact pinned source end to end and independently verified the PDF and extracted-text SHA-256 values. The OpenReview identity is preserved, but its automated PDF/API routes currently return a browser challenge; the pinned source override is the official arXiv v2 PDF 2110.03677, whose title, authors, 45-page length, ICLR 2022 journal reference, and page-one conference banner match the OpenReview item. Main text occupies pages 1-9, references pages 10-12, and supplementary Appendices A-I pages 13-45. Rendered and visually inspected every page. The paper contains 17 numbered figures and no tables: Figures 1-4 are in the main text; Figures 5-14 are multi-panel factorization, sensing, and completion experiments; Figures 15-17 cover periodic orbits, modified-equation mismatch, and stability-limit sensitivity. Audited all displayed and numbered equations through Equation 22, all propositions, theorems, lemmas, and proof appendices. High-resolution inspection was used where text extraction lost fraction bars: the balance bounds scale as 2/h, not 2h. The source has no code, dataset, seed list, environment, or machine-readable artifact; targeted official-record, author-page, exact-title, identifier, and GitHub searches found none. A separate reviewer-f18f14b61fc8 pass rechecked the complete source and reconciled the Appendix I block-condition, block-index, and constant-dependence contradictions, the G.17-G.20 anchor, and four current EoS successors. Current primary competitors and successors were checked through 2026-08-24. Confidence is very high in the source, visual, artifact, general-rank contradiction, trace-factor, and theorem-scope audits; high in the scalar and rank-one proof-gap assessment; and moderate-to-high about the truth of the scalar theorem itself because the documented issue is failure of the supplied proof, not a constructed counterexample.
